title: India's First Trade Deal With a Western Economy in Decades Goes Live in Two Weeks. Here's What Changes.
excerpt: The India-UK CETA comes into force on July 15 with tariff cuts, professional mobility provisions and the end of double social security payments for Indian workers in Britain.
body:
Two weeks from today, the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement will come into force. When it does on July 15, it will be the first major free trade deal India has signed with a Western economy in decades — and the first to include provisions specifically designed to ease the movement of Indian professionals into Britain.

Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who spent three days in London last week finalising implementation details with UK Business Secretary Peter Kyle, was characteristically bullish. He brought the largest-ever Indian business delegation to leave the country's shores — 170 businesspeople from across sectors — and launched a first-of-its-kind business utilisation manual, developed by the UK India Business Council and HSBC India, to help companies on both sides hit the ground running.

"I feel redeemed in some sense that what we have finalised is a partnership that is good for both countries, is full of potential, goes beyond the typical trade in goods and services," Goyal told PTI on the sidelines of the UK-India Week 2026. He invoked Prime Minister Modi's phrase — *yahi samay hai, sahi samay hai* (this is the time, the right time) — to describe the moment in bilateral ties.

## What the deal actually does

The CETA, signed last year after nearly three years of negotiations, cuts tariffs on a broad range of goods traded between the two countries. Bilateral trade has already been growing — reaching roughly £47.9 billion (about $56–60 billion) in the four quarters ending Q4 2025, a 10 per cent increase over previous years.

But the deal goes well beyond tariff schedules. It includes a Double Contribution Convention (DCC), also coming into force on July 15, which eliminates the requirement for Indian professionals posted to the UK to pay into both countries' social security systems simultaneously. For the roughly 100,000 Indian professionals working in Britain on various visa categories, and for the companies that employ them, this could mean significant savings.

The agreement also streamlines regulatory coordination and customs procedures, and establishes mechanisms for professional mobility — a diplomatic way of saying it makes it easier for Indian workers with specific skills to take up assignments in the UK.

## The contrast with Washington

The timing is deliberate. India is pursuing two major trade negotiations simultaneously, and the UK deal's smooth trajectory throws into sharp relief just how stuck the US talks remain.

Wendy Cutler, Senior Vice President at the Asia Society Policy Institute, put it plainly: "Despite substantial progress made in recent meetings, concluding a trade deal with India is proving illusive." She pointed to a "serious trust deficit" between New Delhi and Washington and said India is in no hurry to close a deal until it gets clarity on tariff rates, product exclusions and — critically — an assurance that the US will not impose further tariff hikes after an agreement is signed.

"India very much wants a preferential tariff edge over its competitors, so it is in no hurry to conclude until there is further clarity," Cutler said. "Moreover, it is seeking assurances from Washington on no further tariff hikes, which most likely is a bridge too far for the Trump team."

## What it means for the diaspora

For the 1.9 million people of Indian origin living in the UK — the country's largest ethnic minority — the CETA has practical implications that go beyond economic statistics. The Double Contribution Convention alone could save thousands of pounds annually for professionals who currently pay into both the UK's National Insurance system and India's Employees' Provident Fund.

The tariff reductions are also expected to lower prices on specific goods traded between the two countries, from Indian textiles and jewellery entering the UK market to British machinery and medical equipment heading to India.

India has now signed nine trade agreements with 38 countries over the past five years, a pace of deal-making that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago. But few of those deals carry the symbolic weight of this one. The UK was, until 1947, India's colonial ruler. That the two countries have negotiated a modern partnership of equals — one that includes worker mobility provisions that would have been unimaginable during the contentious post-Brexit "hostile environment" era — is itself a measure of how far the relationship has come.

Commerce Secretary Sunil Barthwal has noted that India's merchandise exports rose 18 per cent year-on-year to $45.2 billion in May 2026, and that India is targeting $1 trillion in merchandise exports for 2026-27. The UK deal, while modest in the context of India's total trade basket, adds another building block to that ambition — and one that comes with the added benefit of being fully implemented before the ink is dry on a US agreement that may not arrive for months, if it arrives at all.
